options.text: I think there is serious doubt about whether he would actually win at the ballot box. While the state media in Cairo tries to project an aura of inevitability, ordinary citizens in places like Tahrir Square are growing deeply fatigued by military rule. When you look at the strong grassroots organizing coming out of the Muslim Brotherhood and other civilian factions, a general stepping into the presidency faces a fierce contest, and victory is far from guaranteed for him.
options.why: Answer 1 states there is no doubt Sisi will win and that opponents will withdraw, whereas Answer 2 argues there is serious doubt about his victory due to strong grassroots opposition.

options.text: People have good reason to doubt his chances in the election because powerful opposition networks in Alexandria and Giza still remember the harsher days of the Supreme Council of the Armed Forces, and prominent political figures are already organizing a united front to challenge any uniformed candidate so that if he runs, he will face a formidable campaign that could easily defeat him when voters cast their ballots this spring.
options.why: Answer 1 states there is no doubt that General Sisi will win the election, whereas Answer 2 argues that he faces a formidable campaign that could easily defeat him.

options.text: There is no doubt whatsoever. In fact, many of the other potential candidates have already said that if Abdel Fattah el-Sisi declares his candidacy, they are going to withdraw. The real question is what this means for Egyptian democracy. I think the answer is that it does not bode well to have a military general as president in a country that has had military strongmen ruling for 60 years, and I think that is the great tragedy of all of this.

I have serious doubts about assuming he is unbeatable because the country faces a severe economic crisis and the Tamarod movement and youth groups are holding any future leader to an incredibly high standard. If Field Marshal el-Sisi runs, he will have to answer for persistent shortages and security failures that frustrate voters daily, and a charismatic civilian alternative could easily galvanize enough public anger to pull off an upset against the military establishment.
options.why: Answer 1 states there is no doubt that General Sisi will win, whereas Answer 2 argues there are serious doubts about assuming he is unbeatable due to economic crises and potential voter backlash.

options.text: Cairo ignores American threats completely because Riyadh and Abu Dhabi provide far more financial muscle than the United States ever did. King Abdullah of Saudi Arabia and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan wired billions of dollars straight to our Central Bank through the National Bank of Egypt and Banque Misr. We do not need the State Department or the United States Congress when the Gulf Cooperation Council funds our fuel imports and wheat supplies. Foreign Minister Nabil Fahmy and President Adly Mansour know that Wall Street and the White House are completely irrelevant compared to the oil wealth flowing from the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia.
options.why: Answer 1 argues that the Egyptian government is significantly concerned with American aid and strategic cooperation, whereas Answer 2 asserts that Cairo completely ignores the United States because it relies entirely on financial backing from Gulf states.

options.text: Washington matters deeply to every single minister in Cairo because the Central Bank of Egypt is completely broke right now. Prime Minister Hazem el-Beblawi and Minister of Finance Hany Kadry Dimian spend every waking hour worrying about the Federal Reserve and the World Bank. Without backing from the Treasury Department and President Barack Obama, our currency would collapse tomorrow against the euro and the British pound. The Export-Import Bank and the Overseas Private Investment Corporation are the only things keeping the stock exchange in Heliopolis afloat. If the United States Ambassador Anne Patterson decides to cut off the aid package, the whole cabinet would resign within forty-eight hours.
options.why: Answer 1 argues that Egypt holds significant leverage and the U.S. needs Egypt just as much, while Answer 2 argues that Egypt is entirely dependent on U.S. financial backing and would immediately collapse without it.

options.text: The military as an institution receives $1.3 billion a year in aid from the United States, and being on good standing with the United States provides other benefits, such as when dealing with the IMF for a loan. At the same time, in some ways the United States needs Egypt more than Egypt needs the United States, which explains why the present administration has been relatively silent on the abuses we have seen. They need Egypt to maintain the Camp David Peace Treaty, because of the importance of the Suez Canal, and because of the unlimited overflight rights Egypt grants the United States military.

The ruling establishment is terrified of the United Nations and the European Union, not the United States government. Chancellor Angela Merkel of Germany and President François Hollande of France hold actual leverage over our tourism sector in Sharm el-Sheikh and Luxor. When the European Parliament in Brussels passes a resolution condemning the Ministry of Interior and General Mohammed Ibrahim Moustafa, our stock market actually drops. British Petroleum and Eni from Italy have billions invested in our natural gas fields off the coast of Alexandria and Port Said. Washington is just a paper tiger; the real economic pressure comes from London, Paris, and Berlin, which buy our petroleum and manufactured goods.
options.why: Answer 1 argues that the Egyptian government is significantly concerned with the United States due to military aid and strategic leverage, whereas Answer 2 claims the establishment is unconcerned with the U.S. and fears European economic pressure instead.
